newsitem.title: USA: IBM posts third quarter profit of $1.3 billion.
newsitem.headline: IBM posts third quarter profit of $1.3 billion.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. said Monday it earned $1.3 billion in the third quarter, up from a loss of $500 million a year ago when it was paying for its acquisition of Lotus Development Corp.
IBM said its income meant earnings of $2.45 a share, just above Wall Street's average estimate of $2.43, and came on revenue of $18.1 billion, which was 8 percent ahead of a year earlier.

"This was a very good quarter," said Louis Gerstner, chairman. "A highlight was the continued rollout of integrated solutions that help fulfil the promise of a networked world to our customers," he said.

IBM's stock initially retreated after the results were released but rallied later after the company's chief financial officer gave an optimistic outlook for the company. The stock was up $4.125 at $133.50 a share in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange after reaching an earlier peak of $135.375, a new high for the year.
Chief Financial Officer G. Richard Thoman said in a meeting with analysts that he was "very comfortable" with the computer giant's prospects for 1996.
"I feel very good about the quarter and very good about the year," Thoman said.

In the third quarter of 1995, excluding the costs of the Lotus acquisition, IBM earned $1.3 billion, or $2.30 a share, on revenues of $16.8 billion. The one-time charge related to its acquisition of Lotus was $1.8 billion.
The company said revenues were higher in North America, Asia and Latin America but were flat in Europe. Revenue at its services division increased by 26 percent, IBM said.

Revenues in North America were $8.2 billion, up 14 percent, Asia Pacific was up 8 percent to $3.5 billion, Latin America rose 12 percent to $811 million. Europe was essentially flat at $5.6 billion. Excluding currency effects, Asia-Pacific was up 19 percent.

Total hardware sales were $8.4 billion, up 8 percent year over year. PC sales, AS/400 minicomputers, and storage systems were up, while RS/6000 work stations, mainframes, and semiconductors fell. Service revenues were up 26 percent to $3.9 billion.

IBM said pricing pressures hurt its semiconductor business. Software revenues were off 1 percent to $3.1 billion, largely due to a decline in host-based software, which runs on mainframes. Distributed software revenues grew significantly vs. a year ago. Maintenance revenues fell 7 percent to $1.8 billion.

For the first nine months, IBM earned $3.84 billion, or $7.16 a share, on sales of $52.8 billion. A year earlier, the company earned $4.25 billion, or $7.39 a share, on sales of $50 billion. Year-earlier figures included a chage of $435 million related to IBM's acquisition of Tivoli Systems Inc., and Object Technology International Inc.
